title: Chinese Beef and Potato Stew

title: One-Pot Pumpkin Mushroom Rice
subtitle: Vegetarian pot or rice-cooker meal
creator: Jeeca (The Foodie Takes Flight)
ingredients: 0.7 oz dried shiitake mushrooms, soaked overnight or in hot water for 30 minutes, then thinly sliced. Reserve soaking water
Neutral oil, for cooking (quantity not specified)
1 green onion, sliced, white and green parts separated
1/2 lb pumpkin, peeled and cut into small chunks or cubes
5.2 oz shimeji mushrooms or other fresh mushrooms, ends trimmed and mushrooms separated
1 cup (200 g) uncooked short-grain or Japanese sushi rice, washed
1/2–1 tbsp soy sauce, to taste, with more after cooking if desired
1/2 tbsp dark soy sauce, optional, for color
1 cup reserved mushroom soaking water, plus 2–3 tbsp additional water if needed
Sliced green onions, to finish (quantity not specified)
Chili oil, to finish (quantity not specified)
Crispy fried shallots, to finish (quantity not specified)
steps: Soak the dried shiitake overnight, or in hot water for 30 minutes. Reserve their soaking water, then slice the mushrooms thinly.
Heat a drizzle of neutral oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Sauté the white parts of the green onion with the garlic for 1–2 minutes, until fragrant.

Add the pumpkin and a pinch of salt. Cook until golden and lightly charred at the edges, then remove and set aside. For firmer pumpkin, cook it for less time or skip this sauté and add it raw when layering the rice.
Sauté the shiitake and shimeji in the same pot until browned and fragrant, then set them aside with the pumpkin.
Add the washed rice, soy sauce, optional dark soy sauce, vegetarian oyster sauce, mirin and 1 cup mushroom soaking water to the pot. Mix to distribute the seasonings.

Layer the pumpkin and mushrooms over the rice without mixing. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-low heat, then reduce to low and cook for 20–22 minutes, until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed. If it dries out before the rice is cooked, add 2–3 tbsp water and keep steaming over low heat.

Switch off the heat and let the pot stand, covered, for 5 minutes. Alternatively, place the seasoned rice and liquid in a rice cooker, layer the pumpkin and mushrooms on top, and cook on the regular or white-rice setting.
Fluff the rice and gently mix in the vegetables. Finish with sliced green onions, chili oil and crispy fried shallots.

title: Steamed Egg Custard
subtitle: Silky, tofu-like Chinese steamed egg
creator: Eric & Lulu
imageCredit: Photo: Tam3415, via Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0
ingredients: About 1 cup plus 2 tbsp water or broth, based on the measured egg volume
A few drops of toasted sesame oil, optional
steps: Gently stir the eggs with the salt until fully combined. Do not whip in air.
Measure the beaten eggs, then stir in 1.5 times that volume of water or broth. Three large eggs are about 3/4 cup, so use about 1 cup plus 2 tbsp liquid.
Strain the mixture through a mesh strainer into a heatproof serving bowl. Skim off any surface bubbles.
Cover the bowl with foil or a small plate so condensation cannot pit the surface.
Steam gently over low to medium heat for 12 to 15 minutes. It is done when the center is just set and wobbles like soft gelatin without sloshing.
Remove from the heat and finish with a few drops of sesame oil and sliced scallion greens. Serve warm.
evidence: The recommended ratio is 1 part beaten egg to 1.5 parts liquid for a very soft, silky texture. Use a 1-to-1 ratio for a firmer, more tofu-like custard.
Straining removes stringy egg bits and helps produce a smooth surface.
Gentle heat matters most. High heat creates bubbles, a spongy texture and watery pockets.
Water works well. A little beef broth gives the custard more flavor.

Garnish with green onion and sesame seeds, then serve with rice.
For a regular pot, simmer the ribs and sauce covered over low heat for about 1 1/2 hours. Add the vegetables and cook about 30 minutes longer, until tender.

title: Avgolemono Soup
subtitle: Greek chicken, rice, lemon and egg soup
creator: Kelly (Kelly's Clean Kitchen)
ingredients: Salt and pepper, to season (quantity not specified)
Olive oil, for sautéing (quantity not specified)
Minced parsley, to garnish (quantity not specified)
steps: Season the chicken thighs with salt and pepper, then set them aside.
Warm olive oil in a pot over medium heat. Sauté the onion, carrots and celery, salting as you go, until translucent, about 5–8 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for another 2 minutes.

Pour in the chicken stock and add the bay leaf and thyme. Season with salt and pepper. Bring to a gentle simmer, add the chicken and rice, cover and simmer over low heat for 20 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through.
Lift out the chicken, shred it with forks and return it to the pot.

Whisk the egg yolks (or whole eggs) with the lemon juice until smooth. With the soup simmering, slowly whisk hot broth into the egg mixture one ladle at a time, using 4–6 ladles to heat it gradually. The recipe specifies bringing the mixture to 160°F. Do not pour the hot broth in quickly, which can scramble the eggs.
Whisk the warmed egg mixture back into the simmering soup until combined and thickened. Taste, adjust the seasoning and finish with minced parsley.
evidence: Adapted from the creator’s written recipe. Listed timing is 10 minutes prep and 30 minutes cooking, for 4 servings.
Salt, pepper, olive oil and parsley quantities are not specified. The source allows 2 whole eggs instead of 4 yolks.
Temper the eggs gradually with 4–6 ladles of broth. The source gives a 160°F target for the egg mixture. This does not mean eggs cannot curdle if overheated.
Food-safety note from Food Vault, not a change to the source recipe: check that the chicken reaches 165°F before shredding.

title: Classic Braised Taiwanese Beef Stew
subtitle: 紅燒牛肉 · Short ribs, potatoes and carrots
creator: Tiffy Cooks
ingredients: 3 lb boneless beef short ribs, cut into 2-inch pieces
1 tbsp Sichuan peppercorns, optional, for blanching
1/4 cup Chinese cooking wine, used in the blanching step
Cold water, enough to cover the beef for blanching
Cooking oil, for browning (quantity not specified)
2 large carrots, peeled and cut into chunks
6 cups beef stock (the instructions also allow water)
4–5 star anise pods, optional, for stewing
2 tsp Sichuan peppercorns, optional, for stewing
4 tbsp water, for the optional cornstarch slurry
Cooked rice, to serve (quantity not specified)
steps: Put the beef in a pot with the Chinese cooking wine and, if using, the 4 ginger slices, 2 green onions and 1 tbsp Sichuan peppercorns. Add enough cold water to cover.
Bring to a simmer over medium heat and cook for 5–10 minutes, skimming off scum. Drain the beef, rinse it under cold water, pat dry and set aside.
Heat cooking oil in a large pot. Add the beef and brown it on all sides for 2–3 minutes.
Add the sliced onion and sauté for 3–4 minutes, until softened and fragrant. Stir in the smashed garlic and cook for another 30 seconds.
Stir in the tomato paste, doubanjiang, soy sauce, dark soy sauce and sugar. Cook for 2–3 minutes, stirring frequently.
Add the 6 cups beef stock (or water), bay leaves and the optional stewing spices: 2 tsp Sichuan peppercorns and 4–5 star anise pods. Stir well and bring to a simmer.
Lower the heat to medium-low, cover and braise for 2–3 hours. Stir every 30 minutes to keep the bottom from sticking.
Add the potatoes and carrots. Cover and cook until they are tender, about 20 minutes.
For a thicker sauce, mix the optional 2 tbsp cornstarch with 4 tbsp water, stir the slurry into the stew and cook until it reaches the desired consistency. Serve hot over rice.
evidence: Adapted from Tiffy Cooks’ written recipe and ingredient card. The source lists 6 servings and about 3 hours, without a prep-time estimate. Allow additional time if needed for blanching, browning and the vegetable stage.
This recipe contains doubanjiang, a spicy fermented bean paste. It is not bean-free. The ingredient is retained rather than silently substituted.
Blanching uses 1 tbsp optional Sichuan peppercorns. Stewing uses a separate 2 tsp optional Sichuan peppercorns. The cooking wine goes into the blanching water.
Beef shank or brisket can replace the short ribs according to the source. Cooking oil and serving rice have no stated quantities. The cornstarch slurry is optional.

title: Nepali Style Chicken Chukauni

steps: Combine the chicken with ginger-garlic paste, salt, pepper, Kashmiri chili powder, turmeric and lemon juice. Marinate for 10–15 minutes. The source does not explain how the listed salt, turmeric and chili powder are divided between stages.

Add the sliced onion, chopped green chilies and half the coriander to the chicken. Mix and set aside.
In a separate bowl, whisk the curd or Greek yogurt with garlic paste, salt and sugar until smooth. The amount of salt for this stage is not specified.

Heat the mustard oil. The supplied source says to heat it until smoking hot, then turn off the heat and add turmeric, Kashmiri chili powder and crushed kasuri methi. It does not give turmeric or chili-powder quantities for this stage. See the safety note below before heating the oil.
Pour the hot tadka into the yogurt and swirl gently to leave streaks.
Pour the yogurt mixture over the chicken and mix gently. Finish with the remaining coriander and serve with soft rotis or hot rice if desired.

title: Taiwanese Pork Rib & Daikon Soup
subtitle: 排骨蘿蔔湯 · Clear broth with ginger and garlic
creator: Eating Alone Diaries
imageCredit: Supplied pork rib and daikon soup photo. Original photographer not identified.
ingredients: 1 lb pork ribs, cut into bite-size pieces
1 lb daikon radish, peeled and cut into chunks
About 8 cups water for the soup, enough to cover the ingredients, plus water for blanching
Scallions or cilantro for garnish, optional. Quantity not stated.
steps: Put the pork ribs in a pot and cover with cold water. Bring to a boil and cook for 3–4 minutes, until foam and impurities rise to the surface. Drain and rinse the ribs under running water.
Return the cleaned ribs to a clean pot. Add the daikon, ginger and garlic, then pour in fresh water to fully cover the ingredients, about 8 cups.
Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Cover and cook for 45–60 minutes, until the pork is tender and the daikon is soft and slightly translucent. Skim off any foam that appears.
Season with salt and white pepper to taste. Stir gently and simmer for another 2–3 minutes.
Ladle into bowls, garnish with chopped scallions or cilantro if desired, and serve hot.
evidence: Imported from supplied recipe text for the linked Eating Alone Diaries article. The source page blocked automated access, so the supplied text is the transcription evidence rather than an independent live-page verification.
The text gives 3–4 servings, a 3–4-minute blanch, a 45–60-minute covered simmer and a final 2–3-minute simmer after seasoning. Prep and total time are not stated.
The source recommends seasoning near the end and keeping the simmer gentle for a clearer broth. Daikon contributes natural sweetness.
Optional variation from the supplied text: add carrots or corn for extra sweetness. No quantities are specified for these additions.
The source describes this as part of a multi-dish Taiwanese meal rather than necessarily a standalone entrée.
